narrative:
The model determined that you have a 93.3% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and wants students likely to pass, this strong prediction of failure led directly to the rejection of your application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the greatest impact. Placing in the bottom decile for both Year 1 and Year 3 grades pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. These low rankings, compared to an average around the middle of the class for accepted students, signaled that you may struggle with the demands of law school and the bar exam.

Your LSAT score of 31 was the third most influential factor. This score is noticeably below the average of 37 for admitted students and also contributed to the prediction of failure, though to a lesser extent than your academic rankings.

Taken together, these academic signals outweighed other details such as your high family income, undergraduate GPA of 2.7, and full-time study plans.

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Building a stronger record in these core areas will help future applications demonstrate a higher likelihood of passing the bar. (218 words)
